claims.text: The target Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially has a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing microstructure.
Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys tend to develop intermetallic compounds during microstructural evolution.
Aging the target alloy at 200°C for 10 hours will precipitate intermetallic compounds.
Aging-induced precipitation can strengthen multi-principal-element alloys.
Spinodal decomposition participates in the aging transformation pathway of the target Mg-containing alloy.
Chemical short-range order participates in the aging transformation pathway of the target Mg-containing alloy.
Spinodal decomposition and chemical short-range order cause aging strengthening.
Aging the target alloy at 200°C for 10 hours will strengthen it relative to the unaged initial state.
Aging the target alloy at 200°C for 10 hours will retain its high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial state.
Aging the target alloy at 200°C for 10 hours may reduce its corrosion resistance relative to the initial state.
Precipitated intermetallic compounds cause the predicted loss of corrosion resistance.
A controlled atmosphere will prevent oxidation during aging.
The relevant boundary is defined only as the temperature and time limits of the aging treatment.
The controlled comparison is between the 200°C/10-hour aged alloy and the same alloy without aging.
Microhardness, electrical resistivity, and tensile strength will be measured in the comparison.
Failure to observe both aging strengthening and retention of high-temperature oxidation resistance would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism field specifically assigns spinodal decomposition and chemical short-range order, while the uncertainty field says the exact transformation mechanism is unresolved. This is a tension between a definite mechanism assignment and stated mechanistic uncertainty.
